summary: An announcement that UCSB offered a Data Reconfiguration Service, an experiment in reformatting data streams passing between two network programs. Users define a form describing changes such as inserting or deleting fields, packing characters, or translating character sets. The RFC explains how to use the service.

plainLanguage.summary: A translator box that sits between two computers and rearranges the information passing through so each one can understand the other.

questions: what was the data reconfiguration service
how does drs reformat network data
subtitle: A service for reformatting data streams between incompatible network processes.

tldr.problem: Network processes with different input and output formats cannot easily communicate with each other, even though the data they need to exchange is semantically similar.
tldr.mechanism: The Data Reconfiguration Service (DRS) sits between two processes and transforms the data stream according to rules defined in a user-written form, handling operations like field insertion, deletion, character packing, and character set translation.
tldr.outcome: Two incompatible processes can communicate as if directly connected, with the DRS transparently reformatting data between them.

today: The DRS is a historical experiment in network protocol adaptation from the early 1970s. The service is no longer operational, but it demonstrates an early approach to handling protocol incompatibility between network processes.

sections.title: The Data Reconfiguration Service
sections.content:
RFC 437 announces the Data Reconfiguration Service (DRS), an experimental service at the University of California, Santa Barbara that reformats data flowing between network processes. DRS provides a solution to a key problem: processes on the network often have different input and output interfaces, making it difficult for them to communicate even when they need to exchange the same information.

The DRS allows a user to define a form, a set of rules describing how to transform data. DRS then establishes network connections with two processes, reads the data stream from one process, applies the form to reformat it, and sends the result to the second process. To the two processes, it appears they are directly connected to each other.
sections.plainLanguage: A service at UCSB that acts like a translator between two computers on the network, reading messages from one and sending them to the other with the information rearranged.

sections.title: Forms and Transformations
sections.content:
A form is a user-written description of the transformations to apply to data. Forms specify operations such as inserting fields, deleting fields, processing variable-length strings, computing string lengths, transposing fields, packing or unpacking characters, and translating between character sets. The DRS system comprises three major components: a compiler that translates form source code into machine-independent instructions, an interpreter that executes those instructions, and the DRS Time Sharing System (DRS/TSS) that manages user access to the service.

DRS supports both simplex (one-way) and duplex (two-way) connections between processes. In duplex mode, two forms can be applied, one to each direction of data flow, allowing complex bidirectional transformations.
sections.plainLanguage: A form is like a recipe that tells the translator what changes to make: keep this part, delete that, rearrange things, change characters, and so on.

sections.title: Accessing DRS/TSS
sections.content:
Users connect to the DRS Time Sharing System (DRS/TSS) through socket 1281 using Telnet. The system provides commands for creating and storing forms, invoking the compiler or interpreter, and managing jobs. When a user connects, they are assigned a TTY number. Commands include DEFINE to create a form, COMPILE to compile it, RUN to execute it with specific network connections, and various administrative commands for managing files and sessions.

The RFC details the complete command syntax, control characters for editing, and parameters for specifying network connections. Connection parameters allow the DRS to either wait for incoming connections (acting as a server) or initiate connections to other hosts (acting as a client).
sections.plainLanguage: You log into the DRS/TSS system and type commands to define your transformation form, compile it, and tell it which two computers should be connected.
